reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: An oesophageal web is a thin, eccentric mucosal membrane composed of squamous epithelium and lamina propria, typically arising from the anterior wall of the cervical (upper) oesophagus just below the cricopharyngeus.
Most webs are asymptomatic incidental findings; symptomatic webs cause intermittent, non-progressive solid-food dysphagia because they only partially occlude the lumen.
The classic association is Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Brown-Kelly) syndrome: a cervical web with iron-deficiency anaemia and dysphagia, seen predominantly in middle-aged women.
Barium swallow with careful lateral views of the cervical oesophagus is more sensitive than endoscopy, which can rupture a thin web before it is recognised.
Webs differ from Schatzki rings by location (cervical versus distal), circumferentiality (webs are usually partial and eccentric, rings circumferential) and histology (webs are squamous-lined only).

Simple mechanical disruption during endoscopy or through-the-scope balloon or bougie dilatation is usually curative, and correction of underlying iron deficiency should accompany treatment in Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
Plummer-Vinson syndrome carries an increased long-term risk of post-cricoid and upper oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, warranting surveillance awareness.

Multiple or lower webs, or webs with mucosal fragility, should raise suspicion of an associated dermatological or immune disorder such as epidermolysis bullosa or a mucocutaneous blistering condition.
reference.pathophysiology: An oesophageal web is a protrusion of normal mucosa (stratified squamous epithelium over vascular connective tissue of the lamina propria) into the lumen, without a muscular component, producing a shelf-like partial obstruction. In the cervical oesophagus the aetiology is often idiopathic but is strongly linked to chronic iron deficiency, where impaired iron-dependent oxidative enzyme activity in rapidly regenerating mucosal cells is thought to promote atrophy and abnormal epithelial healing with web formation. Webs may also be congenital, or acquired secondary to chronic mucosal injury from gastro-oesophageal reflux, eosinophilic oesophagitis, graft-versus-host disease, mucocutaneous blistering disorders (epidermolysis bullosa, cicatricial pemphigoid, lichen planus) or prior caustic or radiation injury. The partial luminal narrowing impedes passage of a solid bolus while liquids pass freely, explaining the characteristic intermittent solid dysphagia.
additionalDifferentials: eosinophilic oesophagitis with rings or strictures
extrinsic compression (cervical osteophyte, aberrant vessel, thyroid mass)
additionalInvestigations: barium swallow with dedicated lateral and anteroposterior cervical oesophageal views
full blood count with iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation) to detect iron-deficiency anaemia
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with careful inspection of the cervical oesophagus
oesophageal biopsies where eosinophilic oesophagitis or a mucocutaneous disorder is suspected
high-resolution oesophageal manometry if a motility disorder is considered
evaluation for occult blood loss and coeliac disease when iron deficiency is unexplained
redFlags: progressive rather than intermittent dysphagia, suggesting stricture or malignancy
weight loss, odynophagia or anorexia raising concern for carcinoma
haematemesis or evidence of significant gastrointestinal blood loss
a neck mass or hoarseness suggesting post-cricoid or laryngeal malignancy
recurrent aspiration or an inability to manage secretions
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent for isolated webs, which usually resolve with simple dilatation and correction of iron deficiency, though recurrence can occur. Patients with Plummer-Vinson syndrome require awareness of a heightened long-term risk of upper aerodigestive squamous cell carcinoma.
pitfalls: Missing a thin cervical web on endoscopy because it is inadvertently disrupted or lies just below the upper sphincter before careful inspection.
Failing to investigate and correct underlying iron deficiency, so that dysphagia recurs.
Attributing all dysphagia to the web without excluding a coexisting motility disorder or malignancy.
Overlooking the malignancy risk in Plummer-Vinson syndrome and omitting appropriate follow-up.
Confusing a web with a Schatzki ring and mislocating or mistreating the lesion.

management: Mechanical disruption of the web by endoscopic through-the-scope balloon or bougie dilatation, which is usually curative
Correct underlying iron deficiency with iron replacement, central to Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Brown-Kelly) syndrome
Investigate and treat the source of iron deficiency, including occult gastrointestinal blood loss and coeliac disease
Treat any contributing mucosal disease — reflux with acid suppression, eosinophilic oesophagitis, or a mucocutaneous blistering disorder
Dietary advice for dysphagia with careful chewing and adequate fluids around dilatation
Follow-up for symptom recurrence, which may require repeat dilatation
In Plummer-Vinson syndrome, maintain awareness of the heightened long-term risk of upper aerodigestive squamous cell carcinoma with appropriate surveillance
